title: HPDT Phar11/195P — Ann Tiller (Pharmacists)
text:
Level 13, Mid City Tower, 139 Willis Street, Wellington 6011
PO Box 11649, Manners Street, Wellington 6142, New Zealand
Telephone: 64 4 381 6816 Facsimile: 64 4 802 4831
Email: gfraser@hpdt.org.nz
Website: www.hpdt.org.nz
DECISION NO: 425/Phar11/195P
IN THE MATTER of the Health Practitioners
Competence Assurance Act 2003
AND
IN THE MATTER of disciplinary proceedings against
ANN TILLER, pharmacist of
Christchurch
BEFORE THE HEALTH PRACTITIONERS DISCIPLINARY TRIBUNAL
HEARING in Christchurch on 1 December 2011
TRIBUNAL: Mr B A Corkill QC (Chairperson)
Ms M O'Rourke, Ms E McCrae, Mr D Sayer and Mr Q Hix
(Members)
Ms G Fraser (Executive Officer)
Ms K O'Brien (Stenographer)
APPEARANCES: Mr M McClelland and Ms H Brown, for the Professional Conduct
Committee
Mr H Matthews, for Mrs Tiller

2
Introduction:
1. On 29 September 2011, a Professional Conduct Committee (PCC) appointed by the
Pharmacy Council of New Zealand laid a disciplinary charge against Mrs Tiller. It
related to a media release which was published on 5 December 2010, entitled
"Massive Mark-Ups Make Medicine Difficult for Families to Afford", and which
contained disparaging comments about other practitioners.
2. The charge is as follows:
"1. The Committee charges that Mrs Tiller as the proprietor and pharmacist of the
Community Pharmacy Linwood ("the Pharmacy") is guilty of professional
misconduct in that she has committed acts or omissions that a) amount to
malpractice or negligence in relation to her scope of practice (section
100(1)(a) of the Act) and/or b) that she has committed an act or omission that
has or is likely to bring discredit to the profession (section 100(1)(b) of the
Act).
2. The acts or omissions that the Committee alleges amount to professional
misconduct are particularised below.
Particulars of charge
3. Mrs Tiller practised in an unprofessional manner and/or has brought the
pharmacy profession into disrepute and/or has impaired the public's
confidence in the pharmacy profession, in that:
a on or around 5 December 2010, Mrs Tiller published, or caused to be
published, a media release entitled 'Massive Mark-Ups Make Medicine
Difficult for Families to Afford' ("the media release") (attached as
schedule 1); and
b the media release contained disparaging remarks regarding other
pharmacies that has brought, or was likely to bring, discredit to the
profession; and
c such conduct is contrary to the obligations of a pharmacist under
obligations 7.1, 8.1, 8.2, 8.3, 9.1 and 9.6 of the Pharmacy Council
Code of Ethics 2004.
4. The Committee, pursuant to section 81(2) and 91 of the Act, charges that the
conduct of Mrs Tiller particularised in paragraph 3 above, either separately
or cumulatively, amounts to professional misconduct pursuant to section
100(1)(a) or (b) of the Act."
3. The media release is attached at Schedule 1 to this decision.

3
Legal principles:
4. The burden of proof was on the PCC.
5. As to standard of proof, the appropriate standard is the civil standard, that is proof to
the satisfaction of the Tribunal on the balance of probabilities, rather than the criminal
standard. The degree of satisfaction called for will vary according to the gravity of the
allegations. The greater the gravity of the allegations the higher the standard of proof.
6. Section 100 of the HPCA Act defines the grounds on which a health practitioner may
be disciplined. The Tribunal has now had ample opportunity to consider the test for
professional misconduct under the section, and the approach to it is well settled –
examples of the correct approach are found in Nuttall (8/Med04/03); Aladdin
(12/Den05/04 and 13/Den04/02D) and Dale (20/Nur05/09D).
7. The section provides that malpractice and/or negligence and/or conduct likely to bring
discredit to the profession can constitute professional misconduct.
8. “Malpractice” is defined in the Collins English Dictionary (2nd ed) as:
1. “The immoral, illegal or unethical conduct or neglect of professional
duties. Any instance of improper professional conduct.”
9. In the new shorter Oxford English Dictionary (1993 edition) the word is defined as:
“Law. Improper treatment or culpable neglect of a patient by a physician or of a
client by a lawyer … 2 gen criminal or illegal action: wrongdoing, misconduct.”
10. Malpractice, although often equated with negligence, is perhaps better considered a
broader concept, capable of encompassing neglect, but also of extending to
trespassory conduct in the process of caring for patients in relation to consent,
breaches of patient confidence and fiduciary obligations, and other forms of conduct
reaching the necessary level of gravity, such as assaulting a patient, swearing at or
threatening a patient, a deliberate failure to obey an instruction or sexual misconduct.
(see para 23.65, “Medical Law in New Zealand”, 2006).

4
11. Negligence and malpractice were discussed by Gendall J in Collie v Nursing Council
of New Zealand [2000] NZAR 74. His Honour said:
“Negligence or malpractice may or may not be sufficient to constitute
professional misconduct and the guide must be standards applicable by
competent, ethical and responsible practitioners and there must be behaviour
which falls seriously short of that which is to be considered acceptable and not
mere inadvertent error, or oversight or for that matter carelessness.”
12. Similarly, it is for the Tribunal to decide whether the conduct, if established, would be
likely to bring discredit on the medical profession. In the same case Gendall J stated:
“To discredit is to bring harm to the repute or reputation of the profession. The
standard must be an objective standard for the question to be asked by the
Council whether reasonable members of the public, informed and with the
knowledge of all the factual circumstances, could reasonably conclude that the
reputation and good standard of the nursing profession was lowered by the
behaviour of the nurse concerned.”
13. In IRG v Professional Conduct Committee of the Psychologists Board [2009] NZAR
563, the Court of Appeal emphasised that the intention in enacting section 100 in its
current form was to move away from an approach that differentiated between levels of
seriousness in the charge. The differentiation was now likely to be reflected in the
penalty, not the charge (at [49]).
14. There are two steps involved in assessing what constitutes professional misconduct:
14.1. The first step involves an objective analysis of whether or not the health
practitioner’s acts or omissions can be reasonably regarded by the Tribunal as
constituting:
• malpractice; or
• negligence; or
• otherwise meets the standard of having brought, or was likely to bring
discredit to the practitioner’s profession;
14.2. The second step requires the Tribunal to be satisfied that the health
practitioner’s acts or omissions require a disciplinary sanction for the purposes

5
of protecting the public and/or warrant maintaining professional standards
and/or punishing the health practitioner.
15. This approach to the assessment of professional misconduct under the statute is well
established under previous decisions of the Tribunal, and in authorities such as
McKenzie v MPDT & Anor [2004] NZAR 47.
16. The correct approach to threshold is that described in the Court of Appeal in F v
Medical Practitioners Disciplinary Tribunal [2005] 3 NZLR 774, which endorsed the
earlier statement of Elias J in B v Medical Council (noted at [2005] 3 NZLR 810).
She made the important point that the threshold is “inevitably one of degree”. The
Court of Appeal expressed the issue in this way:
“In cases of both professional misconduct and conduct unbecoming it will be
necessary to decide if there has been a departure from acceptable standards
and then to decide whether the departure is significant enough to warrant
sanction.”
17. In determining whether the departure is significant enough there must be positive
reasons to justify such a conclusion.
18. The Tribunal accepts and applies the above principles, in this case.
Code of Ethics:
19. The Board’s publication Code of Ethics and Standards of Practice (2004) was before the
Tribunal and relied on in support of allegations in the charges.
20. Not all breaches of a Code of Ethics will necessarily constitute professional misconduct;
obviously a fact specific analysis is required and an assessment made as to the seriousness of
the departure, but the principles of such a Code are a helpful indicator of proper practice and
ethical standards. This approach is consistent with statements made in the High Court such
as:
20.1. Staite v Psychologists Board (1998) 18 FRNZ 18, wherein Young J stated that a Code
of Ethics should not be used as a template; rather the principles of the Code should be

6
regarded as a guide, and as one of the factors to be taken into account by the Tribunal
when exercising its independent judgment as to whether in the particular
circumstances there has been professional misconduct.
20.2. To similar effect is the dicta of Smellie J in Lake v The Medical Council of
New Zealand (HC Auckland, HC123/96, 23 January 1998 at p30); and of Gendall J in
Collie (supra) at para 30.
Agreed summary of facts:
21. The charge was able to be dealt with on the basis of an agreed summary of facts, as
follows:
1 Background
1.1 Ann Tiller is a registered pharmacist of Christchurch. At all material
times Mrs Tiller was the owner and charge pharmacist of Community
Pharmacy Linwood (the Pharmacy) in Christchurch. Mrs Tiller
operates the Pharmacy with her husband, Joe Tiller and they are co-
directors of Community Pharmacy Limited.
2 Media release
2.1 On 5 December 2010, Mrs Tiller published, or allowed to be published,
a media release entitled ‘Massive Mark-Ups Make Medicine Difficult
for Families to Afford’ (the media release). A copy of the media
release is attached as Schedule 1.
2.2 The media release related to the prices that pharmacies were charging
for pharmaceuticals and the pricing approach that Mrs Tiller’s
Pharmacy intended to take. Mrs Tiller’s media release also made
comparisons between the Pharmacy and other pharmacies in general
regarding pricing, the benefits received by the community from other
pharmacies, and the level of profit being made by other pharmacies.
2.3 The media release was published in a number of online forums,
including www.infonews.co.nz and www.nzdoctor.co.nz.
2.4 On or around 6 December 2010, the Pharmacy Council of New
Zealand received a complaint from Mr Simon Bensley, proprietor of
QEII Pharmacy in Christchurch regarding the media release.
3 Particulars of the complaint
3.1 Mr Bensley considered that the media release was contrary to the
Pharmacy Council Code of Ethics and that it included comments that
were unprofessional, unethical and cast the profession in bad light.

7
3.2 Mr Bensley was also concerned about the effect the media release
would have on the relationship between pharmacists and patients.
3.3 The specific aspects of the media release that were of concern included
the following:
a The suggestion of ‘price gouging’ by pharmacies.
b The statement that the public are paying ‘far too much’ at
pharmacies and that pharmacies were making large profits.
c The statement that “We have been appalled by the price
charged by pharmacies. What is happening is profiteering;
pure and simple”.
3.4 Mrs Tiller acknowledges that the above statements impaired, or had
the potential to impair, the public’s confidence in the profession.
3.5 The parties agree that the applicable Code of Ethics is the 2004 code.
3.6 Mrs Tiller accepts that the content of the media release was
inconsistent with the following obligations of the Code:
a Obligation 7.1: a pharmacist must uphold reasonably accepted
standards of behaviour both within and outside their
professional practice and must refrain from any conduct that
might bring the profession into disrepute or impair the public’s
confidence in the pharmacy profession.
b Obligation 8.1: the pharmacist must not disparage the
professional services of other pharmacies or pharmacists.
c Obligation 8.2: the Charge Pharmacist must be responsible for
the form and content of any advertisements whether placed by
the Charge Pharmacist personally, or by another staff member
or organisation on behalf of the pharmacy, and for any other
publicity which the Charge Pharmacist expressly authorises.
d Obligation 8.3: the Charge Pharmacist must use only those
methods that are of a standard consistent with the professional
image of pharmacy when advertising, promoting or offering as
inducement to the public any services, interventions, medicine,
complementary therapy, herbal remedy or other healthcare
product.
e Obligation 9.1: The pharmacist must endeavour to foster,
develop and maintain effective relationships with professional
colleagues and other healthcare providers and to cooperate
with them to achieve beneficial medicines related health
outcomes for patients and the community.

8
f Obligation 9.6: The pharmacist must endeavour to maintain
the confidence and trust placed in colleagues and other
healthcare providers by patients and must refrain from making
public comment that could detract from their professional
reputation or harm the relationship they have with patients.
3.7 Mrs Tiller accepts that in the circumstances she has acted in an
unprofessional manner, has brought the pharmacy profession into
disrepute, and has impaired the public’s confidence in the pharmacy
profession.
4 Investigation by Committee
4.1 On 14 February 2011, the Council advised Mrs Tiller’s legal counsel
that a Professional Conduct Committee (the Committee) was to be
appointed to investigate the complaint regarding the media release.
4.2 Further information was received from the complainant on 26 March
2011.
4.3 The Committee also received submissions received on behalf of Mrs
Tiller’s legal counsel dated 6 May 2011, and from Mrs Tiller on 15
June 2011.
4.4 On 9 June 2011, the Committee received a letter from Mr Don Sache,
pharmacist who responded on behalf of Mr Bensley.
4.5 On 8 August 2011, the Committee determined that a charge be brought
against Mrs Tiller before the Tribunal in accordance with section
80(3)(b) of the Health Practitioners Competence Assurance Act 2003.
4.6 A notice of charge was then filed with the Tribunal on 29 September
2011. The full particulars of the charge are contained in the notice.”
22. A bundle of documents containing correspondence from the complainant and
Mrs Tiller and/or her lawyers was also placed before the Tribunal.
Liability:
23. Although Mrs Tiller accepted the facts in the agreed summary of facts and that the
conduct particularised in the charge amounted to professional misconduct, the
Tribunal was required to reach its own conclusion as to whether the conduct amounted
to professional misconduct.

9
24. The PCC submitted:
24.1. The content of the media release could objectively be regarded as
unprofessional and of a nature that reflects adversely on the profession as a
whole.
24.2. References were made to previous Tribunal and Court decisions where a
breach of the Code of Ethics has occurred,1 indicating that the Code can be a
helpful indicator as to whether standards of proper practice and ethical
standards have been breached.
24.3. Each of the relevant principles of the Code were explained with regard to the
present case.
24.4. The media release was in essence advertising on behalf of the pharmacy. It
was targeted at patients and the content related to comparisons between the
pharmacy and other pharmacies, the prices being charged at other pharmacies
and the level of profits being made by other pharmacies. Overall, the
impression gained was a claim that Mrs Tiller's pharmacy was superior in
terms of price and services, and those comments detracted from the reputation
of other pharmacies. Of particular concern were the disparaging references to
"price gouging" and "profiteering".
24.5. The pharmacy profession recognises the importance of collegial relationships
to promote health outcomes for patients, and to ensure that public comments
regarding other professionals are of a nature that do not harm relationships
with patients.
24.6. The complainant indicated he was aware that as a result of the comments in the
media release, significant strain was placed on relationships between a
1 As per para 20 of this decision.

10
pharmacist and a patient, after the patient viewed the media release and made
accusations.
24.7. All pharmacists are expected to be fully cognisant of their obligations and
comply with the standards set by the profession. Here there was a lack of
regard for the professional standards provided in the Code, and the likely
impact on relationships between patients and other pharmacies, which could
jeopardise the public's confidence in the profession and bring the profession
into disrepute.
24.8. The publication of the media release itself does not give rise to breaches of the
Code. The remarks that other pharmacies were "price gouging" however had
the real potential to impair the public's confidence in the profession, regardless
of the fact that no particular pharmacy or pharmacist was identified.
24.9. The actions were serious enough to attract a disciplinary sanction to ensure the
professional standards are maintained.
25. Counsel for Mrs Tiller did not need to make submissions with regard to liability.
Liability - decision:
26. The Tribunal accepts the submissions made for the PCC.
27. It was most unfortunate that statements were made which were strongly critical of
other pharmacists. Those comments did not disparage the professionalism of other
pharmacists, but were disparaging as to the quantum of prices charged by other
pharmacists, and as to the level of profits obtained by other pharmacists.
28. It appears the media release was widely circulated; colleagues reacted and
understandably considered the statements made to be quite unprofessional; there was
also evidence of a patient being affected by the publication.

11
29. Accordingly the Tribunal was satisfied:
29.1. That each of the particulars of the charge were made out; with regard to
paragraph b) of the particulars, the Tribunal accepts that the matters of
particular concern were:
29.1.1. The suggestion of "price gouging" by pharmacies.
29.1.2. The statement that the public are paying "far too much" at pharmacies.
29.1.3. The statement that "We have been appalled by the price charged by
pharmacies. What is happening is profiteering: pure and simple".
29.1.4. Thus there were significant breaches of the obligations in Principles
7.1, 8.1, 8.2, 8.3, 9.1 and 9.6 of the Code of Ethics, as set out in the
Agreed Summary of Facts.
30. These disparaging remarks:
30.1. Amounted to practising in an unprofessional manner.
30.2. Brought the pharmacy profession into disrepute.
30.3. Impaired the public's confidence in the pharmacy profession.
31. For the purposes of section 100(1)(b) of the Act, there was an act or omission that has
or was likely to bring discredit to the profession.
32. The Tribunal concluded that the established conduct was sufficiently serious as to
warrant discipline, in order to uphold professional standards. A clear message needs
to be sent by the Tribunal to all pharmacists that such breaches of the Code of this
nature will not be tolerated.
33. Accordingly the charge of professional misconduct was established.
Penalty:
34. The PCC submitted that an appropriate penalty would be:
34.1. Censure.

12
34.2. An order that Mrs Tiller pay a proportion of the costs of the Committee and the
Tribunal.
34.3. Publication of name.
34.4. It was also appropriate that Mrs Tiller apologise for her conduct, by way of
apology made through the Society, and "Pharmacy Today", and through the
media.
35. As for costs, the amounts involved were:
35.1. For the PCC: $11,400.00 (exclusive of GST).
35.2. For the Tribunal: $12,000.00 (exclusive of GST).
36. For Mrs Tiller it was submitted:
36.1. She had been a pharmacist for 22 years, and had practised for most of that
period; details of her practising history were described.
36.2. Late in 2010, she had established a community pharmacy, as a "discount
pharmacy". The intention was that it would provide choice for members of the
public in the particular location in which it was established.
36.3. This was new to the area, and appeared to have generated considerable concern
for other pharmacists; that had created antagonism and pressure had been
brought to bear on suppliers, to the extent that in one instance a supplier
removed a product from the pharmacy shelves.
36.4. Mrs Tiller had wanted to get the message out as to the nature of her new
pharmacy, and engaged a PR firm to "announce" the business. The PR firm
drafted the media release.
36.5. Although it was not an excuse, the proposed media release was not in
appropriate terms; Mrs Tiller gave the document insufficient attention before it
was published.

13
36.6. She never intended to cast a slur on other pharmacists, although it was
accepted this in fact occurred. She accepted she had "overstepped the mark".
This was an error of judgment and a lack of proper controls at a time of stress.
36.7. Personal circumstances were described to the Tribunal.
36.8. It was emphasised that Mrs Tiller had never previously had difficulties of the
present kind.
36.9. It was accepted that the proposals for resolution of the matter as advanced by
the PCC were appropriate.
37. There was then further discussion with Counsel as to the tendering of an apology, and
it was agreed that this would be attended to in the course of the hearing.
Penalty – legal principles:
38. In determining the appropriate penalties, the Tribunal recognised the following
functions of disciplinary proceedings:
38.1. To protect the public – this object is reinforced by section 3 of the HPCA Act;
38.2. to maintain professional standards – this object is emphasised in Taylor v
General Medical Council [1990] 2 All ER 263; Ziderman v General Dental
Council [1976] 2 All ER 344 and Dentice v The Valuers Registration Board
[1992] 1 NZLR 720;
38.3. to punish the practitioner in question, as referred to in Dentice v The Valuers
Registration Board and Patel v Complaints Assessment Committee (CIV-2007-
404-1818, 13 August 2007 Lang J);
38.4. where appropriate, to rehabilitate the practitioner, as referred to in J v Director
of Proceedings (CIV-2006-404-2188, 17 October 2006, Baragwanath J), and
Patel (supra).
39. In A v PCC (5 September 2008, Keane J, CIV-2008-404-2927), the Court discussed
carefully the range of sanctions available to the Tribunal, particularly cancellation and

14
suspension.2 The Court stated that four points could expressly be derived from the
authorities, and implicitly a fifth:
“[81] First, the primary purpose of cancelling or suspending registration is to
protect the public, but that “inevitably imports some punitive element”.
Secondly, to cancel is more punitive than to suspend and the choice
between the two terms on what is proportionate. Thirdly, to suspend
implies the conclusion that cancellation would have been
disproportionate. Fourthly, suspension is most apt where there is
“some condition affecting the practitioner’s fitness to practise which
may or may not be amenable to cure”. Fifthly, and perhaps only
implicitly, suspension ought not to be imposed simply to punish.
[82] Finally, the Tribunal cannot ignore the rehabilitation of the
practitioner: B v B (HC Auckland, HC4/92, 6 April 1993) Blanchard J.
Moreover, as was said in Giele the General Medical Council [2005]
EWHC 2143, though “… the maintenance of public confidence … must
outweigh the interest of the individual doctor”, that is not absolute –
“the existence of the public interest in not ending the career of a
competent doctor will play a part”.”
40. In numerous cases, the need to consider and explain why lesser options have not been
adopted is emphasised. But the Tribunal has to proceed on the basis of what
is appropriate having regard to the public interest, and the need to maintain public
confidence in the profession.3 Randerson J put the matter in this way:
“[30] The consequences of removal from a professional register are
ordinarily severe and the task of the Tribunal is to balance the nature
and gravity of the offences and their bearing on the dentist’s fitness to
practise against the need for removal and its consequences to the
individual: Dad v General Dental Council [2002] 1 WLR 1538. As the
Privy Council further observed at 1543:
Such consequences can properly be regarded as inevitable where
the nature or gravity of the offence indicates that a dentist is unfit
to practise, that rehabilitation is unlikely and that he must be
suspended or have his name erased from the register. In cases of
that kind greater weight must be given to the public interest and to
the need to maintain public confidence in the profession than to the
consequences of the imposition of the penalty to the individual.
[31] I respectfully adopt the observations of the Privy Council and would
add that it is incumbent on the Tribunal to consider carefully the
alternatives available to it short of removal and to explain why the
2 Paras 77-82.
3 Patel, supra, para 30 per Lang J; L v The Director of Proceedings, Woodhouse J, 25 March 2009, CIV-2008-404-2268
[47-48].

15
lesser options have not been adopted in the circumstances of the case.
As well, while absolute consistency is something of a pipe dream, and
cases are necessarily fact dependent, some regard must be had to
maintaining reasonable consistency with other cases. That is necessary
to maintain the credibility of the Tribunal as well as the confidence of
the profession and the public at large.”4
Penalty – discussion:
41. After the Tribunal had deliberated on the issue of penalty, it was confirmed that an
apology had been prepared which was acceptable to the PCC and that arrangements
had been made for it to be published on an agreed basis.
42. Whilst the Tribunal is of the view that there were significant breaches of the Code of
Ethics (as discussed above), it also considered there were mitigating factors:
42.1. There was no intention to disparage other pharmacists.
42.2. The publication of the document had occurred through lack of proper care;
there was an error of judgment.
42.3. The conduct could be regarded as an isolated aberration.
42.4. Mrs Tiller had dealt with the matter in a responsible way. She had accepted
the conduct was unacceptable, offered no opposition to the charge and
cooperated in having the matter dealt with by way of an agreed summary of
facts.
42.5. She had also taken the constructive step of agreeing to publish an apology, and
to remove, if possible, the original statement from the relevant websites.
43. In all those circumstances the Tribunal concluded that the matter could be dealt with
by way of censure, and an order for costs.
44. The normal starting point for costs is 50% of the reasonable costs incurred; and in a
case such as the present where there had been significant cooperation, it is appropriate
4 Patel v The Dentists Disciplinary Tribunal HC AK AP77/02, 8 October 2002.

16
to make a further allowance. In the present case, 30% of the reasonable costs,
$7,000.00 is an appropriate amount to order.
45. The Tribunal has also taken into account that no application for non publication of
name was made – although in the circumstances of this case, there appeared to be no
grounds which would have justified such an order.
Conclusion:
46. The charge of professional misconduct is established.
47. There is an order of censure; the Tribunal must formally record its disapproval of the
breaches of the Code of Ethics which occurred; members of the pharmacy profession
should be in no doubt that breaches of the Code of this kind are unacceptable.
48. Mrs Tiller is to pay:
48.1. $3,500.00 in respect of the costs of the PCC.
48.2. $3,500.00 in respect of the costs of the Tribunal.
48.3. GST is not payable in respect of either such sum.
49. The Tribunal directs that the Executive Officer publish a copy of this decision and a
summary on the Tribunal’s website. The Tribunal further directs the Executive
Officer to publish a notice stating the effect of the Tribunal’s decision in the bulletin
of the Pharmacy Council, “The Edge” (which is the publication of the Pharmaceutical
Society), the Guild’s website and “Pharmacy Today”. (Section 157 HPCA Act
2003).
DATED at Wellington this 9th day of December 2011

B A Corkill QC
Chairperson
